CAN.story:
From the 1870s until 1997, the Canadian government paid churches to run Indian residential schools, boarding schools that First Nations, Métis and Inuit children were made to attend. About 150,000 children went to them, and the Catholic Church ran more than half. Under a 2006 settlement, former students could claim compensation for sexual and serious physical abuse through the Independent Assessment Process; it received 38,276 claims, and adjudicators awarded $2.14 billion to 23,431 claimants.
In St John's, Newfoundland, the Christian Brothers, a Catholic teaching order, ran the Mount Cashel orphanage. In December 1975, after two Brothers admitted molesting boys, the police chief and assistant chief ordered the detective to end his investigation. References to sexual assault were removed from his report, the Justice Department laid no charges, and four Brothers were moved out of the province. Police reopened the case in 1989 and nine Brothers were convicted. The Hughes Royal Commission, a provincial public inquiry, reported in 1991 that neither the police nor the Justice Department had handled the files normally.

Two priests of the Oblates of Mary Immaculate, a Catholic order with missions in the Arctic, left Canada before trial. Fr Eric Dejaeger fled to Belgium in 1995 when he was about to be charged, and lived in Oblate houses there for 16 years despite an international warrant; after he was returned in 2011 he was sentenced to 19 years for 32 offences against Inuit children in Igloolik. Fr Johannes Rivoire left for France in 1993. Canada issued warrants in 1998 and 2022, France refused to extradite him, and he died there in 2024 without trial.

Under the settlement, the records of residential school abuse claims are to be destroyed after 19 September 2027 unless the claimant asks to keep them. Much of what is known about abuse in Canadian institutions comes from inquiries and compensation claims, and some of the accused were never tried in Canada.

IRL.story:
From the 1930s to the 1990s, Catholic religious orders ran more than 250 industrial schools and other institutions for the Irish state, holding over 30,000 children. The Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse, known as the Ryan Commission, reported in 2009 after nine years of work. It found sexual abuse "endemic" in the boys' institutions, most of them run by the Christian Brothers, a teaching order, and found that Department of Education inspections had failed to stop it. The Christian Brothers sued the commission in 2004 to keep their members' names out, and the report names no abusers. A state redress scheme paid about 12,000 people an average of €65,000.

Inquiries into individual dioceses followed. The Ferns report of 2005 found that Bishop Donal Herlihy moved accused priests to other posts for a time and then reinstated them. The Murphy report of 2009 found that four archbishops of Dublin had not told the Gardaí, the Irish police, what they knew, and that the archdiocese had taken out insurance against abuse claims from 1987. The Gardaí themselves had treated priests as outside their remit. In Cloyne, the 2011 report found that nine complaints made after the church adopted reporting rules in 1996 were not passed to the Gardaí, and said the Vatican's response to those rules had allowed bishops to ignore them.

The Norbertine order moved Fr Brendan Smyth between parishes, dioceses and countries, including the United States, without reporting him. At church meetings in 1975 two teenage victims were sworn to secrecy, and their evidence never reached the police. The Irish government's delay in acting on a request from Northern Ireland's police to extradite him led to the fall of the government in 1994. In 1997 he was sentenced in Dublin to 12 years for abusing 20 children.

In 2024 a state scoping inquiry recorded 2,395 allegations of sexual abuse against 884 alleged abusers at 308 schools run by 42 religious orders, and the government announced a full commission of investigation. More than half of those alleged abusers are dead.

CHL.story:
In 1959 authorities in Siegburg, Germany, issued a warrant for Paul Schäfer for abusing two boys. He fled, and in 1961 he founded Colonia Dignidad, a closed German commune in southern Chile. The colony recruited children from local farms into its free school and clinic. In 1966 a teenager who escaped took refuge at the West German embassy, which sent a delegation and said it found no evidence. Chilean politicians rejected other escapees' accounts in the 1960s because of the colony's ties to those preparing the 1973 coup. After the coup, DINA, the Pinochet dictatorship's secret police, used the colony to hold and torture opponents, as Chile's Rettig Commission reported in 1991. An investigation opened only after Chilean mothers complained in 1997. Schäfer hid in Argentina until 2005, and in 2006 a Chilean court sentenced him to 20 years for sexually abusing 25 children.

From the 1960s to 2000, children were taken from mainly poor Chilean mothers, some of whom were told their babies had died, and sent for adoption in the United States and Europe, including Sweden. The practice peaked under Pinochet. A Chilean judge opened a criminal investigation in 2018 covering about 8,000 adoptions abroad, and a congressional committee concluded the state was responsible. As of September 2023 nobody had been brought to justice.

In the Catholic Church, parishioners reported Fr Fernando Karadima to the archbishop of Santiago in 1984, and Cardinal Errázuriz shelved a church investigation in 2004–05. In 2015 one of his protégés, Juan Barros, was made a bishop. After a Vatican investigator delivered a 2,300-page report, Pope Francis wrote in 2018 that he had made serious errors in judging the situation, and every bishop in Chile offered to resign.

In 2018 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child found the state responsible for grave violations, including sexual abuse, over 40 years in residences of SENAME, the national child protection service.

In 2019 Chile removed the statute of limitations, the legal deadline for prosecution, for child sexual abuse, so old cases can still be brought. No one had been tried for the adoptions abroad by 2023.

PHL.story:
When Clark Air Base, a US military base in Angeles City north of Manila, closed in 1992, the bars around it lost the American soldiers who had been their customers. The same year Manila's mayor, Alfredo Lim, began closing Ermita, the city's main sex-industry district, and many of its businesses moved to Angeles City and took up foreign tourists as customers. In 2025 the US State Department's trafficking report still named Angeles City among the places where sex trafficking frequently occurs. It said most foreign offenders come from Australia, Japan, New Zealand, Britain and the United States, and many are already convicted or charged sex offenders at home.

From 2006 the charity International Justice Mission (IJM) worked with police in several Philippine cities, and by 2016 the number of children trafficked for sex in bars and other establishments there had fallen by 79 to 86 percent. Over 2014 to 2017 the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for child sexual exploitation grew more than twelvefold. Parents, relatives or neighbours were paid by buyers abroad to abuse children in front of a webcam. Because the buyers were abroad, 64 percent of the cases taken up by the police anti-trafficking unit in 2017 began with a referral from a foreign police force. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaking money-laundering law, including failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation in the Philippines. In 2024 Europol, the EU police agency, examined chats between about 12,000 buyer accounts and 100 sellers in the Philippines, gathered over 12 years, and sent leads on 197 buyers to 24 countries.

In 2002 the Catholic bishops apologised and said about 200 of the country's 7,000 priests had committed sexual misconduct over two decades. No national inquiry into abuse in church or state institutions has been found.

IJM estimated that 1 in every 100 children in the Philippines was a victim of online sexual exploitation in 2022. The people paying for it live mostly in a few wealthy countries, so finding them depends on police and banks there.

HTI.story:
From 2004 the UN Stabilization Mission in Haiti, MINUSTAH, included a contingent of about 950 soldiers from the Sri Lanka Army. In 2007 the UN's internal investigators reported that its members had sexually exploited and abused children frequently, usually at night, at almost every place they were posted. A 2017 Associated Press investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had exploited at least nine children between 2004 and 2007. Under UN rules only the country that sends peacekeepers can prosecute them, so the UN could only send the accused home. Sri Lanka took back 114 of them, its authorities judged the acts "consensual", and none was jailed.

Haiti has also sent many children abroad for adoption, 13,986 of them between 2003 and 2022. Most of its orphanages are private and funded from abroad. The charity Lumos found in 2017 that at least US$70 million a year reached about a third of them, that 92 percent of funders were in the United States and 90 percent were faith-based, and that the donations led people to open orphanages and recruit children away from their families. In 2007 one centre was forced to return 47 children it had been holding for adoption after misleading their parents with payments. After the 2010 earthquake, ten American Baptist missionaries were detained while taking 33 children to the Dominican Republic without proper papers; their leader, Laura Silsby, was convicted of arranging illegal travel. In 2019 the government's social welfare agency, after assessing more than 750 orphanages, identified 3,019 children in them as potential trafficking victims.

In 2024 the UN verified sexual violence by armed groups against 566 children in Haiti, up from 41 girls in 2023, and attributed 411 of the cases to the Viv Ansanm gang coalition. The US State Department reported in 2025 that close to half of gang members are children.

Children in Haiti now face sexual violence from gangs, and many still work as restaveks, unpaid domestic servants in other families' homes, where displacement has raised their risk of sexual exploitation.

COD.story:
In 2002 and 2003, during the war in Ituri province in the east, the Union of Congolese Patriots (UPC), an armed group, enlisted children under 15 as soldiers. The International Criminal Court (ICC), which tries people for war crimes when their own country does not, convicted the UPC's leader, Thomas Lubanga, in 2012 of conscripting and using these children; sexual violence against girl soldiers was raised at his trial but not charged. In 2019 the ICC convicted his commander Bosco Ntaganda of crimes including the rape and sexual slavery of child soldiers.

The UN peacekeeping mission sent to the same area was investigated as well. In 2004 the UN's internal investigators found that peacekeepers in Bunia, Ituri's main town, regularly had sex with girls under 18, some as young as 13, in exchange for food or small sums of money. Of 72 allegations, six were fully substantiated, largely because most reports were too vague to investigate. Peacekeepers can only be prosecuted by the country that sent them, and in a 2025 UN report few cases had been finalised. During the 2018–2020 Ebola outbreak in North Kivu and Ituri, aid workers arrived in the same region. An independent commission appointed by the World Health Organization found in 2021 that WHO staff and other responders, mostly local temporary hires, had used offers of jobs to obtain sex, and that the youngest of those it heard was a 13-year-old girl.

The fighting has continued. In 2024 the UN verified sexual violence against 358 girls in the DRC, by the M23 rebel group, the CODECO militia, the national army and others, and the abduction of 815 children. In the eastern mines, the US State Department reported in 2025, mining bosses, family members, officials and armed groups force children into labour, and girls are trafficked for sex and forced marriage.

In eastern DRC, armed groups and the army continue to abuse and abduct children, and few of the commanders, soldiers or responders accused have been tried. No representative survey has measured online sexual exploitation of children in West and Central Africa, which includes the DRC.

GRC.story:
After the Greek civil war, between 1950 and 1975, as many as 4,000 Greek-born children were adopted by families in the United States, the Netherlands and Sweden. Many were described as orphans of the war or had been born to unmarried mothers, and they came from state institutions and foundling homes. AHEPA and other US agencies and intermediaries arranged the adoptions, often quickly and sometimes by proxy, with the adoptive parents not present in Greece. The adoptions were kept confidential, and many adoptees grew up without papers showing where they came from. The Greek state promised an investigation in the late 1950s and never carried it out. On 2 May 2025 a law recognised the adoptees' status, restored a path to Greek citizenship and made it easier for them to see their records.

Greece's own institutions have also been examined. In 2011 the Greek Ombudsman, an official who investigates complaints against public bodies, found that at the state care centre for disabled children at Lechaina, a shortage of staff had led to systematic sedation, children tied to beds and the use of wooden cage beds. In 2014 the BBC found conditions had barely improved. No finding of sexual abuse there was located.

In its 2025 trafficking report, the US State Department said unaccompanied migrant children in Greece are vulnerable to sex trafficking, and that Roma children from Albania, Bulgaria and Romania are forced to beg there.

The adoptees can now reclaim Greek citizenship. The investigation promised in the 1950s has still not taken place, and no wider inquiry into abuse of children in Greek institutions was found.

DNK.story:
In May 1951 the Danish government, working with Save the Children Denmark, asked teachers and priests in Greenland to pick out children aged six to ten. Twenty-two Inuit children were sent to foster families in Denmark to be brought up as "little Danes". About a year and a half later 16 were returned to Greenland and placed in a children's home built by the Danish Red Cross, and many never lived with their families again; six were adopted in Denmark. A 2020 report found that half of them later had mental health problems. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen apologised in December 2020, and in 2022 the six survivors were each awarded 250,000 kroner.

Denmark's state children's homes were examined in the Godhavn Report of 2011, which covered Godhavn boys' home and 18 other homes from 1945 to 1976. It found neglect and physical and sexual abuse, and that about 22 percent of Godhavn's boys had been given psychiatric drugs by a psychiatrist. No prosecutions followed, and Frederiksen apologised in 2019.

Denmark has also received many children from abroad, including 9,297 from South Korea between 1965 and 2008. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found that agencies there had sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign demand and had registered children with known parents as orphans. Denmark suspended adoptions from Ethiopia in 2016 after abuses there, and in 2024 the Danish International Adoption agency, the country's only intercountry adoption agency, said it was closing.

Danish police have led or joined several international investigations of online abuse, from the Bamse bulletin board in the early 1990s to Operation Cumberland in 2025, one of the first cases of AI-generated abuse material, in which 273 suspects were identified.

The children taken from Greenland and those abused in the state homes have received apologies from the prime minister, and the Greenland survivors have been compensated. With its only agency closing, Denmark's part in intercountry adoption is ending.

UGA.story:
From 1987 the Lord's Resistance Army (LRA), a rebel group in northern Uganda led by Joseph Kony, abducted children to use as fighters, porters and "wives" for its commanders. UNICEF estimated that at least 25,000 children had been taken by 2006, and the LRA held many of them at bases in southern Sudan. One of those abducted as a child, Dominic Ongwen, became a brigade commander. In 2021 the International Criminal Court convicted him of 61 crimes, including rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage and the use of children under 15 as soldiers, and sentenced him to 25 years. The court's warrant for Kony has not been carried out.

Uganda also sent children abroad for adoption, 1,933 of them between 2003 and 2022. Between 2013 and 2016 European Adoption Consultants, an agency in Ohio, arranged adoptions of more than 30 Ugandan children by US families. Parents were told their children would go to school in Kampala, and the children were taken to an unlicensed home. An employee pleaded guilty in 2019 to bribing Ugandan officials to obtain adoption orders, and in 2020 two other employees and a Ugandan lawyer were charged and the US government sanctioned two Ugandan judges and two lawyers. Uganda's social development ministry now says only 185 children's homes are licensed and more than 500 operate without oversight, many funded from abroad, and that many children in them are not orphans.

Ugandan soldiers have also been accused abroad. In 2014 Human Rights Watch documented rape and sexual exploitation by African Union soldiers in Somalia, mainly Ugandans, including of girls as young as 12.

Inside Uganda, the US State Department reported in 2025 that most child sex-trafficking victims are Karamojong children from the north-east, whom traffickers, sometimes community elders, sell at markets on the borders. Unlicensed children's homes and cross-border trafficking from Karamoja continue to put children at risk.

CZE.story:
In 2000 and 2001 a Czech court found Fr František Merta, a Catholic priest in the Archdiocese of Olomouc, guilty of abusing more than 20 boys, and gave him a two-year suspended sentence, meaning he did not go to prison unless he offended again. Archbishop Jan Graubner was alleged to have failed to report him to the police and to have moved him between parishes when problems arose. No national inquiry into abuse in the Czech church appears in the records gathered for this map.

Most of the other Czech cases concern abuse images sold abroad. In 2014 Czech police, supported by Europol, the EU police agency, and Eurojust, its agency for cooperation between prosecutors, led Operation Atelier against a Czech photographer. He had photographed close to 70 children from poor and disadvantaged families and, with a Swedish partner, sold the images to customers in the EU and Canada. Ten people were arrested, five of them in the Czech Republic, and 30 terabytes of data were seized. In 2026 Czech police joined police in Norway and five other countries in arresting 28 men suspected of paying cryptocurrency to watch abuse videos on forums reached through anonymising software, after Norwegian police developed a way to trace the payments.

The records for Czechia show one convicted priest and a few international police operations. How many children were abused in Czech churches, schools or children's homes has not been studied.

BLR.story:
In the early 2000s a company in Minsk called Regpay Co. Ltd took paid memberships for about 50 websites, including child abuse sites it ran itself, and sold access to thousands of subscribers around the world. Subscribers paid by credit card, the payments passed through Latvian banks, and a Florida payment firm, Connections, helped hide where the money came from. Because the company was in Belarus, beyond the reach of US police, US agents used a ruse to draw its president, Yahor Zalatarou, and its marketing director to a hotel in Paris, where they were arrested in July 2003; the technical administrator was arrested in Spain and extradited. All three pleaded guilty in New Jersey, and in 2006 Zalatarou and the administrator were each sentenced to 25 years. The customer records led to the arrest of hundreds of subscribers in the US and other countries, in what the US government called Operation Falcon.

Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, children from occupied parts of Ukraine have also been brought to Belarus, about 2,100 of them by 2023. In July 2023 the head of the Belarus Red Cross said the children had come for "health improvement" and that this would continue. In March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin and Russia's children's rights commissioner, Maria Lvova-Belova, for the unlawful deportation and transfer of children from occupied Ukraine to Russia.

How many of the Ukrainian children brought to Belarus have returned home is not recorded in the sources for this map.

BGR.story:
In 2007 a BBC film showed disabled children neglected at Mogilino, a state home for children with physical and mental disabilities. In February 2008 Bulgaria's minister of labour and social policy promised to close Mogilino and six similar homes, and by June children were being moved out with help from UNICEF. Bulgaria has been criticised for keeping one of the highest numbers of children in state institutions in the EU. No finding of sexual abuse at Mogilino was located. In its 2025 trafficking report the US State Department cited a UN special rapporteur, an independent expert appointed by the UN, who found that sexual exploitation, including possible sex trafficking, was common among children in government-run institutions. The same report said traffickers exploit Bulgarian girls and women in Sofia, in resort and border towns and across Western Europe. It found corruption widespread in the police and the courts, and of 31 traffickers convicted, only eight were sent to prison.

Bulgaria also sent 5,067 children abroad for adoption between 2003 and 2022, and its adoptions remain open.

Bulgaria now hosts more of the online abuse material found by the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes such material, than any other country. In 2025 the foundation acted on 87,959 web addresses in Bulgaria, 28 percent of its total, up from 9 percent in 2024, and said most of them belonged to a few particular sites. Bulgarian cybercrime police have also taken servers down, as in 2017–18, when they removed the servers of a subscription site showing the abuse of boys in Thailand.

Children in Bulgarian state institutions remain at risk of sexual exploitation, and most convicted traffickers do not go to prison. In 2025 a few sites hosted in Bulgaria accounted for more than a quarter of the abuse material the foundation found.

SYR.story:
On 3 August 2014 the Islamic State (ISIS) attacked Sinjar, where many Yazidis, a religious minority, lived. Its fighters moved the people they captured by bus and truck to holding sites in Tal Afar, Mosul and Baaj, and then took the women and girls on to Raqqa in Syria. There they were sold at markets and held in sexual slavery, some of the girls as young as nine, and boys were sent to ISIS training camps. In June 2016 the UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria found that ISIS had committed genocide against the Yazidis. At that date more than 3,200 Yazidi women and children were still held, mostly in Syria, and thousands remain missing.

Syrians who fled the war were also exploited in neighbouring countries; Türkiye alone hosted about 2.9 million of them. In Lebanon in March 2016, security forces freed as many as 75 Syrian women from two brothels in Jounieh. Police had raided one of them in 2011, finding a 17-year-old Syrian girl there, and it had reopened about three months later. The US State Department reported in 2025 that Syrian girls in Türkiye are married in unofficial religious ceremonies and then subjected to domestic servitude and sex trafficking, and that Syrian refugee girls in Jordan have been sold into forced marriages.

Inside Syria, the UN verified the abduction of 14 children in 2024 by armed groups and government forces, often to recruit them as fighters.

Thousands of Yazidi women and children taken to Syria are still missing. No representative survey of sexual exploitation of children has been carried out in the Middle East and North Africa, so its scale in Syria and among Syrian refugees is unknown.

BDI.story:
In 2013 and 2014 Burundian soldiers were serving in Somalia with AMISOM, the African Union's peace mission there. Human Rights Watch documented in 2014 cases of sexual exploitation and abuse by soldiers at the Burundian base in Mogadishu, alongside cases involving Ugandan troops. Many of the women and girls had come to the bases to ask for medicine or aid, and some were pressured into sex in exchange for money, food or medicine.

Soldiers on such missions can be tried only by their own country. In the Central African Republic, Burundian and Gabonese soldiers served with MINUSCA, the UN mission there. In 2016 the UN recorded two allegations from the town of Dékoa involving these contingents, which led to interviews with about 136 alleged victims, almost half of all victims the UN recorded that year. UN data list allegations against Burundian personnel involving 46 children. The UN's 2017 report said the investigations by Burundi and Gabon were still pending, and press reports said 41 soldiers were identified and sent home without being charged.

Within Burundi itself, little is recorded. In 2025 the US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, which receives reports of online abuse material from technology companies, received 1,028 reports linked to Burundi, one of the countries from which almost no reports reach the international systems.

No trial in Burundi of the soldiers sent home from the Central African Republic is recorded. Because so few reports come out of Burundi, the extent of abuse of children inside the country is not known.

BGD.story:
In its 2025 report on trafficking, the US State Department said that traffickers take Bangladeshi women and girls for sex trafficking in India, Pakistan and the Gulf states, and observers estimate that children are 40 percent of the Bangladeshi sex-trafficking victims exploited abroad. In India, police in Kolkata rescued nine girls under 18 from a house in the north of the city in September 2025 and charged the couple running it; the State Department says significant numbers of Bangladeshi and Nepali women and girls are recruited for sex trafficking in India.

Near Cox's Bazar, more than one million Rohingya refugees live in 33 camps. Many fled Myanmar, where a UN fact-finding mission found that the army raped hundreds of Rohingya women and girls during its 2017 operations. In Bangladesh, tourists have increased the demand for sexual exploitation near Cox's Bazar, including of Rohingya girls, and the State Department described corrupt policing in the camps. Bangladeshi courts convicted 103 traffickers in the year covered by the 2025 report, down from 407.

Bangladesh was also one of the countries from which children were adopted into the Netherlands. In 2021 a Dutch government inquiry found serious violations in adoptions from Bangladesh and other countries between 1967 and 1998, and the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption.

Girls continue to be taken from Bangladesh and exploited near the camps, and fewer traffickers are being convicted. No representative survey of online sexual exploitation of children has been carried out in South Asia.

GIN.story:
In 2001 a joint mission by the UN refugee agency, UNHCR, and the charity Save the Children UK visited refugee camps in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone. Its report in early 2002 said refugee children were being sexually exploited by employees of aid groups and UN agencies and by peacekeepers, often in exchange for food and aid. The UN Office of Internal Oversight Services, the UN's internal investigators, then examined 43 cases in full and substantiated 10. They included the rape of a 14-year-old refugee girl in a Guinean camp and a UN Volunteer's sexual relationship with a girl of about 15 in Guéckédou. The investigators said in October 2002 that they had found no evidence of "widespread" abuse, and Save the Children UK replied that nothing the UN had found made it think its report was wrong.

Guinea was also the site of Mamou Alliance Academy, a boarding school for the children of missionaries of the Christian and Missionary Alliance (C&MA) working in West Africa. Former pupils wrote to the church's headquarters about abuse from the 1980s, and an inquiry was set up only after 30 of them asked for one in 1995. In 1998 an independent commission found that the church had been negligent and identified nine offenders, whose abuse included sexual molestation and rape. The church's US board then wrote an open letter asking the victims' forgiveness.

Both cases were found by inquiries set up by the organisations involved. No representative survey of sexual exploitation of children has been carried out in West and Central Africa, so its extent in Guinea is not known.

BFA.story:
In 2024 the UN verified the abduction of 309 children in Burkina Faso. Armed Islamist groups took most of them, 157 by JNIM and 80 by ISGS, the Islamic State in the Greater Sahara, and 47 were taken by groups that could not be identified. The other 25 were abducted by the state's own security forces and the Volunteers for the Defence of the Homeland (VDP), civilian auxiliaries who fight with them. It also verified the rape of four girls that year, two of them by the VDP, and in 2022 the rape of 16 girls, two by state forces.

Children from Burkina Faso have also been trafficked across borders. In 2019 police in Kaduna, in northern Nigeria, raided a building presented as an Islamic school and freed more than 300 boys and men, many of them in chains; some had been brought from Burkina Faso, Mali and Ghana, and local media reported that captives had been sexually abused. The US State Department reported in 2025 that Nigerian networks move women and girls to mining areas in several West African countries, including Burkina Faso, for sex trafficking.

Children in Burkina Faso are abducted by both the armed groups and the forces fighting them. No representative survey of sexual exploitation of children has been carried out in West and Central Africa, so its wider extent is not known.

ARE.story:
Telegram, the messaging service, has its operational centre in Dubai. In August 2024 French investigators charged its founder, Pavel Durov, with offences including suspected complicity in running a platform used to share images of child sexual abuse, and with refusing to give information to the authorities. A BBC investigation that month found that Telegram had not joined the US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children or the Internet Watch Foundation, two organisations that collect and share records of known abuse images, and had ignored repeated requests to do so. In December 2024 Telegram agreed to use the Internet Watch Foundation's list of known images to detect them in public parts of the platform. The foundation said it had confirmed thousands of reports of abuse images on Telegram since 2022.

UAE police have taken part in international operations against people sharing abuse images. In 2015 they were one of ten members of the Virtual Global Taskforce, a group of police forces, that together arrested 303 people and identified 106 victims in Operation Atlas.

No other cases from the UAE appear in the records for this map. No representative survey of sexual exploitation of children has been carried out in the Middle East and North Africa, so how many children in the UAE are affected is not known.

VIR.story:
The financier Jeffrey Epstein owned Little St. James, a private island in the US Virgin Islands, and used it as one of the homes where he and Ghislaine Maxwell sexually abused and trafficked girls, some as young as 14, between at least 1994 and 2005. Maxwell was convicted in 2021, and Epstein died in 2019. After his death the territory's government brought civil cases. It reached a $105 million settlement with Epstein's estate and a $62.5 million settlement with the billionaire Leon Black. In December 2022 it sued JPMorgan Chase, Epstein's bank, claiming the bank had ignored warning signs and made his activities possible by keeping him as a client. In 2023 JPMorgan agreed to pay $290 million to nearly 200 of Epstein's victims and $75 million to the Virgin Islands. In 2020 New York's financial regulator had fined Deutsche Bank $150 million for ignoring warning signs about Epstein.

Where the girls brought to the island came from is still being examined. In December 2025 prosecutors in Ankara opened an inquiry after a Turkish MP cited a 2009 civil complaint that alleged Epstein brought girls from Turkey, the Czech Republic and other countries; no findings or charges have been reported.

The Virgin Islands recovered money through civil settlements, which carried no criminal findings, and no bank was criminally charged over Epstein. How many girls were brought to the island, and from where, is still not established.

TLS.story:
In 1992 Richard Daschbach, a US-born missionary priest of the Society of the Divine Word, a Catholic order, founded the Topu Honis children's shelter in Oecusse, a district of Timor-Leste. After a complaint to his superiors in February 2018 he admitted to them that he had abused children there, and the Vatican dismissed him from the priesthood in November 2018. The church did not tell the public. He was arrested in April 2019 and charged with 14 counts of sexually abusing children under 14. A report by the Justice and Peace Commission of the Dili archdiocese defended him, and in December 2021 a court in Oecusse sentenced him to 12 years.

In 2019 the Vatican received allegations that Bishop Carlos Ximenes Belo, a member of the Salesian order and a winner of the Nobel Peace Prize, had abused boys in Fatumaca and Dili before and during his time as bishop. In 2020 it barred him from contact with minors and with Timor-Leste and limited his movement and ministry. It did not announce this, and confirmed the sanctions only in September 2022, the day after the Dutch magazine De Groene Amsterdammer published the accounts of two men. Belo had left Timor-Leste in 2002 and worked in Mozambique from 2004.

In both cases the church learned of the abuse and acted internally without telling the public, and the cases became known through a criminal court and a magazine. Belo has not been tried.

URY.story:
In the 1970s the military governments of Argentina, Uruguay and other South American countries cooperated in hunting down their opponents, under an arrangement known as Operation Condor. In August 1976 a pregnant 19-year-old Argentine woman was detained in Buenos Aires and secretly moved to Montevideo by a joint Argentine–Uruguayan unit. She gave birth in a military hospital, and in December 1976 her baby was taken from her and left with the family of a police officer, who raised the girl under another identity for 23 years. The mother disappeared.

In 1986 Uruguay passed the Expiry Law, an amnesty that protected military and police officers from prosecution for crimes under the dictatorship, and in 2003 it was used to close the investigation into this case. In 2011 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, the court that rules on whether American states have kept their human rights treaties, found Uruguay responsible for the mother's enforced disappearance and for hiding the child's identity, and ruled that the amnesty could not be used to block the investigation.

After the 2011 ruling the amnesty could no longer be used to close this case. It is the only Uruguayan case in the records for this map, so how many other children were taken in Uruguay under the dictatorship is not shown here.

MHL.story:
From 2015 to 2019 Paul Petersen, an adoption lawyer who was also the elected assessor of Maricopa County, Arizona, paid recruiters to bring about 40 pregnant Marshallese women to Arizona, Utah and Arkansas. He paid the women about $10,000 each to give up their babies and charged the adoptive couples about $35,000. This broke the Compact of Free Association, the treaty between the Marshall Islands and the United States, which bars Marshallese citizens from travelling to the US to give up a child for adoption. He also obtained about $814,000 in Arizona Medicaid funds, the public health insurance for people on low incomes, for the women by fraud. He was charged in all three states in October 2019, pleaded guilty in June 2020 to human smuggling and fraud, and was sentenced in December 2020 to more than six years in prison.

The case was prosecuted in the United States. Records from the Marshall Islands of how many children were taken through such schemes are not in the sources for this map.

QAT.story:
On 13 August 2025 Qatar blocked access to Roblox, an online game platform popular with children, after parents and community groups raised concerns about children's safety on it. Kuwait's telecoms regulator blocked the platform temporarily later that month, and Oman and Jordan had banned it since 2020.

No other cases from Qatar appear in the records for this map. No representative survey of sexual exploitation of children, online or offline, has been carried out in the Middle East and North Africa, so how many children in Qatar are affected is not known.

GUM.story:
In 2016 Guam lifted the statute of limitations, the legal deadline for bringing a civil lawsuit, for child sexual abuse, so people abused decades earlier could sue. More than 200 lawsuits followed against the Catholic Archdiocese of Agaña, naming 35 priests, teachers and scoutmasters for abuse going back to the 1950s. In March 2018 a Vatican tribunal found the former archbishop, Anthony Apuron, guilty of charges including the sexual abuse of minors, and rejected his appeal in February 2019. He was removed from office and barred from living in Guam, but remained a priest, and he denies the allegations.

In January 2019, facing the lawsuits, the archdiocese filed for bankruptcy, which placed all the claims in a single court process and limited what it would pay to what a judge approved. The number of claims rose to nearly 280. In January 2020 the archdiocese offered a plan worth $21 million, and it sold a property in Yona for $6.1 million.

Survivors' claims are being settled through the bankruptcy court. The only judgment against Apuron in these records came from a church tribunal.

DJI.story:
In its 2025 trafficking report, the US State Department said that traffickers bring Ethiopian girls into neighbouring countries, particularly Djibouti and Sudan, and exploit them in domestic servitude and sex trafficking, sometimes using drugs to control them. The report said officials continued to be reported as complicit.

No other cases from Djibouti appear in the records for this map. No representative survey of sexual exploitation of children has been carried out in the Middle East and North Africa, the region in which the survey researchers grouped Djibouti, so the number of children affected there is not known.

ERI.story:
Eritrea's army, the Eritrean Defence Forces, was among the forces that fought in the war in Ethiopia's Tigray region from 2020. In 2022 the International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia, a UN-appointed inquiry, documented widespread sexual violence by Ethiopian and Eritrean forces in Tigray, and by Tigrayan forces against women and girls as young as 11 in neighbouring Amhara. In February 2021 the BBC reported that 200 girls under 18 had registered at health facilities in Mekelle, in Tigray, as survivors of rape.

Almost nothing is reported from inside Eritrea. In 2025 the US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, which receives reports of online abuse material from technology companies, received 11 reports linked to the country.

No Eritrean soldier is recorded in these sources as having been tried for the sexual violence in Tigray, and abuse of children inside Eritrea goes almost entirely unrecorded.

KGZ.story: In 2009 Kyrgyzstan suspended intercountry adoption, the adoption of its children by families abroad, and in April 2010 the US State Department issued an alert to American families about the suspension. The records for this map give no reason for the suspension and contain no other cases from Kyrgyzstan, so the scale of abuse and trafficking of children there has not been documented here.

DZA.story: No cases of networked abuse or trafficking of children in Algeria appear in the records gathered for this map. Childlight, a research institute that collects survey data on sexual exploitation of children, found in 2026 that no representative survey of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation of children had been carried out in the Middle East and North Africa, which includes Algeria. How many children there are affected is therefore not known.

Childlight, a research institute that collects survey data on sexual exploitation of children, found in 2026 that no representative survey of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation of children had been carried out in the Middle East and North Africa, which includes Egypt. How many children there are affected is therefore not known.

TKM.story: No cases of networked abuse or trafficking of children in Turkmenistan appear in the records gathered for this map. In 2025 the US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, which receives reports of online child sexual abuse material, mostly from American technology companies, received 591 reports linked to Turkmenistan, which places it among the countries from which almost no reports reach the international systems. With so few reports, the extent of abuse of children in Turkmenistan is not known.
